imageCaption: Anthony's pegboard, propped against Luisana's journal on the living room table, with the blank impossible plate catching afternoon light—the engraving now shows faint outlines of a harbor and colonial architecture.
text:
The second vision came to Anthony on Sunday afternoon, while he was sorting vegetables in the kitchen and humming a song that had no business existing yet.

Aaliyah knew it was a vision because her father had learned to recognize them the same way other people learned to recognize hunger—suddenly, completely, with the kind of certainty that made him go still while holding a sweet potato.

"Lulu," he said, not turning around. "Come look at this."

Luisana appeared in the kitchen doorway with the speed of someone who'd learned that Anthony's sudden silences usually meant something important had happened to the license plate collection. She was holding her phone in one hand and a cup of coffee in the other, which meant she'd been in another late-night Willemstad real estate conversation and hadn't bothered to sleep through it.

"What am I looking at?" she asked.

Anthony held up the plate.

The blank plate—the impossible one that had sat empty on his pegboard since they'd started this journey—was no longer blank.

It had developed details. Faint outlines, like someone had started etching a drawing and decided to pause halfway through. But Aaliyah could see what it was supposed to be. She could see the colonial architecture. She could see the curve of a harbor. She could see, with absolute certainty, the shape of somewhere her parents had been dreaming about separately but together, the way married couples do when they're too cautious to say the dream out loud.

"Curaçao," Luisana whispered. She set down her phone and coffee like they'd become too heavy to hold. "It's actually Curaçao."

"It was always going to be Curaçao," Anthony said quietly. He was still holding the plate like it might disappear if he stopped paying attention to it. "But now it's... concrete. Now it's the next place. The second sancocho. The second Sunday. It's telling us when."

"Plates don't prophecy," Aaliyah said, which was fair, because they didn't, and yet this one apparently did. "Plates are physical objects. They don't develop engravings based on—" She stopped. Because she'd just realized what this meant. "The resonance frequency. The emotional resonance. Dad and Mom have been thinking about Curaçao so hard that it's become stable enough to manifest."

"Your mother's been researching house prices at 3 AM," Anthony said. He was smiling. "Your father's been saving photos of the harbor. That's not a weak emotional resonance, that's a frequency loud enough to reshape metal."

Luisana took the plate from him with trembling hands. She turned it over, looking for any explanation that made sense. There wasn't one. Just the faint outlines of somewhere they'd never been but had been imagining together, so consistently, so specifically, that the timeline had decided to make it real.

"We have four Sundays," Luisana said. "Four sancochos before we leave New York. And then—"

"And then we go to Curaçao," Anthony finished. "Not because the algorithm told us to. Not because the app scheduled it. Because we cooked a meal that got so good, so real, that it literally rewrote our trajectory."

Elijah appeared in the kitchen like he had a sixth sense for moments that mattered. "Is the plate doing something weird?" he asked. He'd already learned to recognize the expression his parents got when the impossible became visible.

"The plate knows where we're going," Aaliyah said.

Elijah took this information with the gravity it deserved. He studied the faint outlines of Curaçao, nodded like the plate had just explained something he'd suspected for a while, and then he asked the only question that actually mattered:

"Can Sully come?"

"Obviously Sully comes," Anthony said. He was holding Luisana, who was having the specific kind of cry that people do when they realize their secret has been so loud it's been heard by time itself. "Sully gets a vote on everything. He's the emotional resonance anchor. He's the reason we even—"

He stopped. Because something had shifted.

Sully had wandered into the living room and had done something that Aaliyah had never seen him do before. He was barking—not his warning bark, not his curious bark, but a sustained, patient, almost musical bark. The kind of bark that sounded like joy translated into sound.

And as he barked, the pegboard shimmered.

Just for a moment. Just long enough that Aaliyah saw it clearly. The plates—all of them, every miniature license plate they'd collected across their journey—glowed briefly with their own light. Like they were remembering everywhere they'd been. Like they were all pointing to the same destination.

"Oh," Luisana said. She was still crying, but differently now. Still surprised, but also unsurprised, the way you get when something you've been hoping for turns out to be so obvious you can't believe you didn't see it the first time. "The resonance route. It's not random. It's not scattered places that happen to stabilize glitches. It's a path. It's all been a path."

"To Curaçao," Aaliyah said slowly. "Fourteen addresses in New York. Four Sundays of sancocho. And then Curaçao. And the plates are the map."

"The plates are the proof," Anthony corrected. He was looking at his collection like he was seeing it for the first time. Every single plate a piece of evidence that they'd been walking toward this exact moment. "We've been collecting the route the whole time. We just didn't know we were reading it backwards."

Sully's bark shifted, became one long sustained note of pure agreement. The kind of bark that sounded like a dog who understood that his family had finally figured it out.

Elijah walked over to the pegboard and pointed at the faint Curaçao plate. "So this one becomes real," he said. "This one becomes solid. And then we go get the yellow house and the afternoon light in the kitchen, and Mom stops researching late at night because she'll be actually living in it, and Dad gets to be spontaneous somewhere he's going to stay."

"Exactly," Anthony said.

"When?" Elijah asked.

"After the fourteenth Sunday," Luisana said. She was smiling now, full smile, the kind that made her look like someone who'd just discovered she'd been home the entire journey. "After we've cooked fourteen meals for fourteen addresses. After we've proven that chaos can build something. Then we leave for Curaçao."

"That's four months," Aaliyah said. She was running the calendar in her head. Four Sundays in August, four in September, four in October, four in November. November. They'd leave in November. They'd arrive in Curaçao as the weather turned cold everywhere else. They'd arrive as a family that had learned how to cook joy into something solid enough for a community to hold onto.

"Four months," Luisana echoed. "Four months of building. Four months of proving that the best journeys are the ones you build together."

The plate caught the light again—just once, just enough that Aaliyah saw the confirmation in it. The timeline was satisfied. The resonance route was real. The Gomez family had finally stopped running from place to place and started building toward somewhere.

And it was going to take exactly four months to get there.

Outside, the August afternoon was perfect. The kind of perfect that felt like the world was holding its breath before it exhaled toward autumn. Sully was barking at something only he could see—probably Abuela Ida's butterfly, probably the timeline checking in to confirm that yes, the family had finally figured it out.

"Let's make something special for dinner," Anthony said. "Something that tastes like the beginning of a plan."

"Plans are for people who don't know what they want yet," Luisana said. But she was already reaching for her journal, already preparing to document this moment. "We're not people with plans anymore."

"We're people with a route," Aaliyah said. "And a timeline that's helping us draw it."

Elijah raised his hand like he was in class. "And we're people with Curaçao," he said. "And a yellow house with kitchen light. And a dog who understands barking."

Sully barked agreement.

And the pegboard, still glowing faintly in the afternoon light, confirmed that every plate had always been pointing toward home.
